You are a read-only security reviewer helping a lead auditor. Do NOT edit, create or delete any file under /tmp/bench/wt/ (no code edits, no tests written), do NOT run git commands that change state, and do NOT run cargo (the lead runs all builds). You MAY write throwaway Python scripts under /tmp/bench/sec1-scratch/access-utils/ for arithmetic checks and run them with `python3 -I`.

Codebase: OpenZeppelin Contracts for Stylus (Rust, Stylus SDK 0.10.10), worktree /tmp/bench/wt/sec1, a port of OpenZeppelin Solidity v5. Your area:
- contracts/src/access/** (ownable.rs, ownable_two_step.rs, control/mod.rs, control/extensions/enumerable.rs)
- contracts/src/finance/vesting_wallet.rs
- contracts/src/utils/** EXCEPT utils/storage_slot.rs, utils/address.rs, utils/cryptography/*, utils/precompiles/* and utils/nonces.rs (the lead covers those). So: utils/pausable.rs, utils/metadata.rs, utils/introspection/erc165.rs, utils/math/{alloy.rs, storage/*}, utils/structs/{bitmap.rs, checkpoints/*, enumerable_set/*}.
Read every non-test line in these files (tests too, when they inform expected behaviour). Compare with OpenZeppelin Solidity v5.x Ownable, Ownable2Step, AccessControl, AccessControlEnumerable, VestingWallet (+ VestingWalletCliff if present), Pausable, ERC165, Math (mulDiv with rounding, sqrt, average, etc.), BitMaps, Checkpoints (Trace160/208/224: push ordering, lowerLookup/upperLookup/upperLookupRecent, latest, latestCheckpoint, length, at), EnumerableSet.

Stylus semantics to keep in mind:
- A `#[public]` entrypoint returning Err reverts all state changes of that call. A panic also reverts. BUT internal Rust composition does not: if library code mutates storage and then returns Err to a Rust caller that handles the Err and continues, partial writes persist. Flag library code paths that catch an Err from a mutating function and continue.
- No Solidity inheritance: e.g. AccessControlEnumerable wraps/embeds AccessControl; check that every path that grants/revokes a role keeps the enumerable sets in sync (including `_grant_role`/`_revoke_role` being callable directly on the inner AccessControl, renounce, set_role_admin). Ownable2Step embeds Ownable: check that every path that changes the owner clears the pending owner (Solidity's Ownable2Step overrides `_transferOwnership` to `delete _pendingOwner`) -- including renounce_ownership and any direct use of the inner Ownable; a pending owner must not be able to accept after a renounce or after a direct transfer.
- External calls (VestingWallet releasing ERC-20 via SafeErc20, releasing ETH via a call): check effects-before-interactions ordering, `released` accounting, reentrancy assumptions (reentrancy is off by default; feature `reentrant` enables it), and value handling. Vesting math: vested = total_allocation * (timestamp - start) / duration, with total_allocation = balance + released; check overflow (U256 multiplication: does it panic or wrap in this build? check what operators/helpers are used), duration == 0, timestamp before start/after end, u64 conversions, start + duration overflow.
- ruint/alloy U256 arithmetic: `+`/`*` on ruint `Uint` panic on overflow in debug and wrap in release? Verify by reading ruint 1.20.1 source at /Users/pepe/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/ruint-1.20.1/src (look at the `Add`/`Mul` operator impls) and report precisely. Release profile has debug-assertions = false and overflow-checks default (false).

Your task:
1. Write down the invariants each contract in your area must keep (examples: Ownable: only owner calls only_owner functions; owner never set to zero except by renounce; Ownable2Step: only the pending owner can accept; pending owner cleared on every ownership change; AccessControl: only admins of a role grant/revoke it; renounce only for self with confirmation; DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE is its own admin; events correct; Enumerable: get_role_member_count(r) == number of accounts with has_role(r); VestingWallet: released(token) <= vested_amount; sum released never exceeds total received; release pays the beneficiary/owner; Pausable: when_paused/when_not_paused; Checkpoints: keys non-decreasing, lookups return the right value at boundaries; EnumerableSet: contains/at/length consistent after any add/remove sequence, values_slice clamping; BitMap: get/set/unset index math; Math: mul_div exact rounding and overflow; ERC165 IDs).
2. Attack each invariant by reading the state-changing code paths: missing checks, wrong order, off-by-one (binary searches!), overflow/underflow, wrong error, access-control gaps, mismatches with Solidity semantics, events with wrong args.
3. For every suspected bug: file:line, what breaks, a concrete trigger scenario (step by step), impact, severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low/Informational) with justification, confidence, a sketch of a unit test (TestVM-based; harness: `TestVM::default()`, `T::from(&vm)`, `vm.set_sender`, `vm.set_block_timestamp`, `vm.set_balance`, `vm.mock_call`, `vm.get_emitted_logs()`; fixtures ALICE, BOB, CHARLIE, DAVE in contracts/src/test_utils.rs; proptest can be added) that would FAIL on the current code and pass after a fix, plus the suggested fix.
4. List every #[ignore]d test in your area and classify it.

Be rigorous: verify each claim against the actual code (quote the lines). Do not report speculative issues as bugs; put uncertain ones in a "needs verification" list. Report invariants that HOLD briefly with the reason. Final answer: a structured report (invariants with held/broken, suspected bugs, needs-verification list, ignored tests). No length limit, but be precise.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.
